references.entry: Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre, Dept. of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Government of India, “YES-TECH Manual 2023: Yield Estimation System based on Technology under PMFBY,” 2023.
references.verification: Downloaded from the official MNCFC site; 116 pages; OCR'd in full and quoted passages located by page. Re-verified verbatim 2026-10-11: clause 3.3.10 (30% floor, states may go higher) and 'at the smallest administrative unit, i.e., Gram Panchayat (GP)'. Document Control Sheet: Document Type 'Implementation manual', Control Number DAFW/MNCFC/PMFBY/YES-TECH/Manual_V1.0, Issue no. 01, Date of Initiation 21 Oct 2022, Date of Publication 11 Jul 2023. ncfc.gov.in/manual.html lists this as the only YES-TECH manual.
references.supports: 30% minimum weightage, no upper cap, Gram Panchayat as smallest unit, court/RTI provisions, commission-error bound
references.uncertainty: RESOLVED 2026-10-11. A separate 48-page 'Manual for Implementation' (MNCFC/DAFW, January 2023, no version number, retrieved from apsac.ap.gov.in) also circulates and carries a hard criterion absent here: clause 4.3.6, 'The error (nRMSE) between the observed and modeled yield should not be more than 30% in historical data. All IUs where the error is more than 30% should not use this methodology.' The 116-page document cited here postdates it by six months, is the versioned V1.0 Issue 01 release, and is the only YES-TECH manual published on MNCFC's own manual page, so it governs. Verified by search of the OCR that the 116-page manual contains NRMSE only in lists of accuracy metrics to report (7 occurrences) and does NOT contain the phrase 'not be more than 30' or any equivalent binding accuracy floor.

references.type: Parliamentary answer (primary government record, not peer-reviewed)
references.verification: PDF retrieved from sansad.in on 2026-10-12; text extracted with pdftotext and read in full. Lok Sabha Starred Question No. 25, 'Pending Claims of PMFBY', to be answered on 21 July 2026; answer by the Minister for Agriculture and Farmers Welfare (Shri Shivraj Singh Chauhan), statement laid on the Table. Quoted verbatim: 'mandatory 30% weightage to yield estimation has been assigned to YES-TECH derived yield. However, State Government of Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra has given 100% and 50% weightage respectively to YES-TECH based yield in 2025-26.' Also: 'Enrolled farmer has no need to file the claims. Claims of enrolled and eligible farmers are automatically worked out based on the shortfall in yield as reported by the State Government concerned.'
references.supports: Madhya Pradesh 100 % and Maharashtra 50 % weightage to YES-TECH yield in 2025-26; 30 % mandatory minimum; claims computed automatically from the area yield under the area approach
references.uncertainty: None on the quoted text. Primary record. It does not say whether any farmer missed a claim, and is not cited for that.

references.type: Presentation of a qualitative field assessment (not peer-reviewed)
references.verification: Presentation PDF retrieved from the CSE site on 2026-10-12 and its text extracted in full. Title slide: 'Learnings from select districts towards improved claim settlement against crop losses as part of Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY)', Chhavi Mahaur, Sustainable food systems programme, Centre for Science and Environment. Field assessment of about 50 farmers in Sehore, Vidisha and Bhopal, plus officials and insurers. Recorded: large soybean farmers reporting a decline in claims; insurers' view that 'there was room for 20-30 per cent error'; officials describing the technology-based process as opaque. The CSE report page on the same study is dated 18 May 2026.
references.supports: That the accuracy of technology-based yield in Madhya Pradesh is contested by farmers and conceded to carry error by insurers; the claim formula Claims = [(TY - AY)/TY] x Sum Insured as presented there
references.uncertainty: SECONDARY and qualitative; small convenience sample. The full report sits behind a registration form and was not read. Cited for the existence and content of stakeholder positions, not for any rate.

references.entry: R. Burnell et al., “Rethink reporting of evaluation results in AI,” Science, vol. 380, no. 6641, pp. 136–138, 2023.
references.verification: 2026-10-13: bibliographic record read from the University of Leeds White Rose repository (eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/198211): 16 authors, Science 380(6641):136-138, DOI 10.1126/science.adf6369. Author-accepted PDF text extracted and read; it states that aggregate metrics make it hard to predict how a system will perform in a particular situation, and that the instance-by-instance results that could unpack them are rarely made available. references.uncertainty: None on the record. Policy Forum argument, not an empirical study; cited for the argument only.

references.entry: M. Stigler, A. Dey, A. Hobbs, and D. Lobell, “With big data come big problems: Pitfalls in measuring basis risk for crop index insurance,” arXiv:2209.14611, 2022.
references.verification: 2026-10-14: arXiv abstract page read: four authors in this order, v1 of 29 Sep 2022 is the only version, no journal reference. The first author's research page lists it under current working papers. It is NOT the AJAE article by Stigler and Lobell, 'Optimal index insurance and basis risk decomposition: an application to Kenya' (DOI 10.1111/ajae.12375), which is a different paper. Abstract: field-level yield data with many fields and few years give downward-biased basis-risk estimates and so overstate insurance quality; shown with satellite-based yields for the US and Kenya and with simulations.
references.supports: That a panel of many fields and few years can make an insurance index look better than it is. Cited in V-E as related evidence, with the difference in question stated.
references.uncertainty: Working paper; findings not peer-reviewed. Cited for its stated argument only.

references.entry: A. Paliwal and M. Jain, “The accuracy of self-reported crop yield estimates and their ability to train remote sensing algorithms,” Front. Sustain. Food Syst., vol. 4, 25, 2020.
references.verification: 2026-10-14: Frontiers article page read. Wheat, rabi 2014-15, Arrah district, Bihar, smallholdings under 0.3 ha. About 73 % of farmers under-reported yield (mean 568 kg/ha); satellite models calibrated on self-reports predicted crop-cut yields with R2 = 0.05 (not significant). Self-reporting and crop-cut farmers were different groups.
references.supports: That self-reported yields can be a poor basis for calibrating field-level satellite yield models. Cited in the label-quality limitation.
references.uncertainty: One district, one season, wheat; transfer to recalled paddy yields in the Cauvery Delta is not shown.

references.entry: D. B. Lobell et al., “Eyes in the sky, boots on the ground: Assessing satellite- and ground-based approaches to crop yield measurement and analysis,” Amer. J. Agr. Econ., vol. 102, no. 1, pp. 202–219, 2020.
references.verification: 2026-10-14: Crossref record read (7 authors: Lobell, Azzari, Burke, Gourlay, Jin, Kilic, Murray; AJAE 102(1):202-219, 2020). Findings read from the abstract of the same team's World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 8374 (DOI 10.1596/1813-9450-8374): large discrepancies among farmer reports, sub-plot crop cuts and full-plot harvests on smallholder maize plots in Uganda, largest for farmer reports; satellite estimates explained as much or more of the variation in full-plot yields as the other measures.
references.supports: That farmer-reported yields can diverge from measured yields. NOT cited as evidence that satellite yield estimation fails: the same study finds satellite estimates competitive, and the text says so.
references.uncertainty: AJAE full text not read; findings taken from the working-paper abstract by the same authors.
